Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Vignette:
Koa, an American of Tongan descent, had been driving back to his hotel after a long layover when a police cruiser pulled him to the shoulder. He had kept his hands on the wheel and lowered his window at the officer’s request, but the moment the door opened and heavy boots hit the pavement, his body locked. The officer stepped close, pressing a knee against Koa’s thigh while searching the console, his voice low and commanding. Koa felt the weight of the stranger’s proximity, the sudden confinement of the cabin, the sharp, unpredictable rhythm of the instructions. It lasted only twelve minutes, but the terror of being trapped by authority never left him. In the months that followed, his perception of the world shifted. Ordinary noises now caught him off guard; a coffee cup clattering on a kitchen counter or a car backfiring down the street made him jerk backward, his breath catching in his throat. Waiting for flight delays or gate assignments triggered a familiar, sinking certainty that something terrible was about to happen, as if time itself were winding toward violence. He stopped inviting anyone to ride with him and grew rigid whenever his brother offered to drive him to the airport, his hands tightening on the armrests, a heavy nausea rising in his stomach whenever the engine pitched up or the road narrowed. His work as an airline pilot, once a source of pride, became a daily calibration of threat monitoring. In the terminal, he found himself leaning away from colleagues who approached from behind, his pulse hammering when ground crew or uniformed security moved into his peripheral vision. During a layover in Phoenix, a fellow pilot tapped his shoulder to check a duty log, and Koa had to step into the hangar just to breathe, his stomach churning until the proximity faded. He began flying lighter schedules, skipping preflight walk-arounds to avoid the sudden shouts of mechanics or the clatter of maintenance equipment. He told himself he was just being cautious, though he knew the hesitation was a shield against another surprise encounter. The memories of the stop did not arrive as distant recollections but as sudden, full-body intrusions. When he closed his eyes between routes, the scene would overlay his cockpit, hyper-real and sharp enough that he could feel the officer’s knee again and smell the hot rubber of the cruiser’s tires. Yet the intensity of those flashes also bred a quiet doubt; he would stare at his flight schedule and wonder if a dream had somehow replaced actual events, as if the terror were too extreme to belong to his own life. He carried this uncertainty alongside the physical toll: the nausea, the startled jumps, the way he now mapped every room for exits, his mind cataloging approaches, delays, and confined spaces. The accumulation of these habits had cost him his marriage; his ex-wife had eventually packed her bags, tired of his sudden flinches and the way he vanished into airports just to avoid the crush of strangers, and the divorce left him navigating layovers alone. What finally brought Koa to a therapist’s office was not a single breakdown but a quiet unraveling during a cross-country red-eye, where a sudden announcement over the intercom sent him gripping the armrest until his knuckles ached, realizing he could no longer outrun the anticipation of dread. He came to the clinic hoping to untangle the knot in his chest, to stop equating every delay with danger, and to reclaim the sky without the constant, heavy nausea of waiting for the other shoe to drop. He just wanted to sit in a car without bracing for impact, and to trust that the past had actually ended.
